docs.text: GlitchyGames is a wrapper around Pygame that aims to support 20-25FPS minimum games on Raspberry Pi and other low powered Linux systems. The engine is written to provide: Readability as a first principle Scene primitives Advanced event handling Human readable/editable sprite file formats Example Game # Let's make a new game called Bitrot Adventures. The goal of our game will be to draw a pixel on the screen and handle key events to move the pixel around. #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Bitrot Adventures""" import argparse import pygame from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class BitrotAdventures ( Scene ): """Draws a pixel to the screen""" NAME = 'Bitrot Adventures' VERSION = '0.0.0' def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options , groups = None ) def main (): # Pass the Scene class uninitialized; the engine creates it GameEngine ( game = BitrotAdventures ) . start () if __name__ == "__main__" : main ()

docs.text: Galimore (1998–2001): what it is and how its tools work # A survey of the Galimore project (1998–2001), the author's earlier game and its tools, made on 2026-10-18 to inform GlitchyGames' level tools ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools.md ). Conventions: SRC/ = the original files ( galimore_files/ , kept outside this repository); X/ = where the survey extracted each archive (one directory per archive). [read] = read directly in a file; [inferred] = concluded from sizes, layouts or context. R/ = PNG renders the survey decoded from the original data with a small read-only decoder, used to confirm the binary layouts below (the decoder and renders are not in this repository). Nothing from the archives was executed. TL;DR # Not a Mac game. Galimore is a top-down tile RPG ("similar to Final Fantasy 3 (English) or Zelda", Galimore Clean Up/Old Galimore Folder/Galimore Archive/public_html copy/index.html ) [read] for MS-DOS , developed on an iMac (Photoshop 5.02 for art, Virtual PC for code: "Yeah, I'm using a Mac to write a PC game", public_html copy/development.html ) [read]. Hence the resource forks, MacBinary .bin , CR line endings and ƒ folder names. Two engine generations: 1999, Borland C++ 16-bit DOS : BGI SVGA256.BGI , 256 colours, XMS. A playable GALIMORE.EXE plus tools GEDIT, GMAP, GATTRIB, MAKEDAT, GTORAW/RAWTOG ( X/CU_galisource072399/ ) [read]. Aug 1999 – Aug 2000, DJGPP (gcc 2.8.1) + Allegro 3.9.32 WIP , 640×480 at 16/15-bit colour. Only the toolchain exists: Galibmap (bitmap/sprite editor), Mapedit (map editor), Galimake (data packer) and a fire-effect demo. The new game was "Not yet started, but should use most of the mapeditor engine" ( development.html ) [read]. Successor: in Aug 2000 the code was relicensed (LGPL) as "RPG Tools" / "Phosphor" , a SourceForge map editor ( Galimore/Old Galimore Folder/RPG Tools Code/ ) [read]; only headers and a Makefile exist (no rendering code; graphics were Allegro 2D, with no OpenGL anywhere). Formats: every file is a raw fwrite dump of a C++ object: no header, no version, little-endian, compiler-specific padding. File type is detected purely by size (2332 / 49152 / 3072 / 4608 bytes). All are fully decoded in §2. 1. Source chronology: 1999-07 BGI ( galisource072399 ) → 1999-10 102599 → 2000-04 gbe/gme_4_17_00 → 2000-05-31 May archive → 2000-06-04/05 codebackup → June daily zips → 2000-07-12 Source 7:12:00 / COMPLETE.ZIP / Archive July 12 (= 08-00 ) → 2000-07-31/08-01 Galimore Source as of 7_31_00 (newest Galimore code) → 2000-08-03 RPG Tools/ (LGPL) → 2000-08-07 RPG Tools Code/ (Phosphor) → 2000-09-05 mapedit (Binary) built → 2001-04-16 Galimore.zip . 7_12 → 7_31: flat directory split into src/ include/ bg/ fg/ get/ raw/ Backup/ ; "cross-platform" exists / file_size in g_io.cpp (later commented out); a GALIMAKE_STUB hack in gmore_raw.cpp ; small fixes in galibmap, g_data and mapedit. 1.3 File counts (2,301 originals) # Art: 845 .raw , 203 .fg , 192 .bg , 46 .gif , 26 .psp , 19 .psd , 14 .get , 3 .spr , 4 .big . Code: 297 .h , 293 .cpp , 75 .o , 25 .gpr + 25 .gdt (RHIDE), 14 .exe . Other: 34 .zip , 11 .map , 10 .dat , 19 .html , 8 .log , ~21 extension-less Mac sound files. .raw sizes: 675 × 3072 (32×32 RGB), 44 × 4608 (32×48 RGB), 118 × 768 (16×16 RGB), 4 × 6144, 4 × 4170. 1.4 Not extracted / unreadable / skipped # Zip members inside ƒ folders failed ("Illegal byte sequence"); their unpacked copies were read. 060400.zip member test<non-ASCII> (a 49,152 B sprite). Nested gbe_4_17_00.zip , gme_4_17_00.zip , gali.zip (May 2000 archive). No unar / lsar ; no StuffIt/BinHex archives found in scope. Sounds: data forks are 0 bytes; audio is only in resource forks ( sfil , System 7 sound). ClarisWorks design docs read via strings only (fragmentary). .psd / .psp / .big identified, not viewed. Skipped as personal: a personal page in public_html copy/ and an e-mail contacts file in RPG Tools Code/ . 2. Tools and file formats # All written with ofstream::write((char*)&obj, sizeof(obj)) , little-endian x86. 2.1 Galibmap: bitmap and sprite editor (2000) # Sources src/galibmap.cpp , src/bmap_gui.cpp , src/gmore_raw.cpp , src/g_object.cpp , src/g_sprite.cpp ; binary X/bitmap_Binary/galibmap.exe . - Space toggles object mode (8 frames of 32×32) and sprite mode (16 frames of 32×48). - 6× zoomed canvas: left-drag paints, right-drag eyedropper; drag frames in the strip to copy or reorder. - R/G/B sliders, three colour wells (C cycles, R replaces colour 2 with colour 1); New / Save / Load / Quit; keys 1–8, N, L, S, Esc. - Load branches purely on file_size : 2332 → object, 49152 → sprite, 3072 → raw tile, 4608 → raw sprite frame (the file browser filters by the same sizes). GALIMORE_OBJECT (tile/object), 2332 bytes ( .bg , .fg , .get ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 2048 | INT16 array[32][32] , [x][y] (offset (x·32+y)·2), RGB565 ; 0xF81F = transparent | | 2048 | 21 | objectName | | 2069 | 1 | objectType | | 2070 | 1 | objectState | | 2071 | 1 | objectSpecial | | 2072 | 2 | objectIsUsableBy (UINT16) | | 2074 | 1 | objectWeight | | 2075 | 256 | objectDescription | | 2331 | 1 | pad | The attribute block is all zeros in every shipped .dat (never authored). GALIMORE_SPRITE, 49,152 bytes ( .spr ): 16 × short array[32][48] , [x][y] RGB565. Frame plan ( spriteguide.html ): front / away / side × still / walk-R / walk-L, side mirrored → 9 used. pockets.spr uses 6 (rest grey). RAW, 3072 / 4608 bytes ( .raw ): headerless 8-bit RGB, row-major , 32×32 or 32×48 (Photoshop Raw export). Pipeline: Photoshop → .raw → Galibmap → .bg/.fg/.get/.spr . 2.2 Galimake: data packer # .dat = 2332-byte records back to back (58,300 = 25×2332, 67,628 = 29×2332, 4,664 = 2×2332). Stable tile IDs: maps store 1-based indices; on update Galimake loads the existing .dat , zeros (doesn't delete) records whose pixels no longer match a file , refreshes matches, and puts new tiles in the first blank slot, so map indices never shift. 2.3 Mapedit: map editor # Sources src/mapedit.cpp , src/mapeditor_gui.cpp , src/g_map.cpp , include/g_map.h . - 14×14 map view with scroll bars; 4×6 tile palette; layer tabs Fgnd / Bgnd / Obj / Spr / Mask ; floor radios 1F / 2F with show-layer checkboxes; "Make a Mask" and "Eraser" (tile 0). - Brush sizes 1–4; s / l save / load; Esc quits. - Mask tab: drag to stamp, right-click to pick up; magenta = no mask, purple = current, black = other. - Mask bits: 0 LAYER_SWITCH, 1 UNPASSABLE_GOOD, 2 UNPASSABLE_BAD, 3 UNPASSABLE_NEUTRAL, 4 DEEP, 5 BRIDGE, 6 CHASM, 7 PUSHABLE, 8 TRANSPARENT. An older plan ( g_mask.h , Dec 1999) added exits, burnable/bombable/freezable, hot/cold, anti-magic, death, door, soil, farmed, layer 2; "Mask Cases" planned a replacement tile in the upper 16 bits (e.g. burnt version) — never implemented. GALIMORE_MAP, 114,692 bytes (arrays [floor][x][y] ; verified by decoding house.map ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 1 | landscape (always 0) | | 1 | 8192 | UINT8 fgLayer[2][64][64] (N → record N-1 of fg.dat ; 0 = empty) | | 8193 | 8192 | UINT8 bgLayer → bg.dat | | 16385 | 1 | pad | | 16386 | 16384 | UINT16 objectLayer → get.dat | | 32770 | 16384 | UINT16 spriteLayer (unimplemented) | | 49154 | 2 | pad | | 49156 | 65536 | UINT64 maskLayer | 64×64 cells per floor, 2 floors. Samples: house.map (cottage on grass, 14 fg tiles, 1 object, 40 fully-impassable mask cells), map.map (lattice test), test.map (18 cells of tile 1). 2.4 The 1999 tools # GEDIT (32×32, 256 colours, rotate/mirror/replace/transparent colour, 8-frame sprites); GMAP (15×15 maps, layer toggles, exits); GATTRIB (attributes); GTORAW / RAWTOG (bitmap ↔ RGB raw, palette as a switch ). The two DOCs are swapped ( GMAP.DOC documents GEDIT). - Bitmap, 1312 B: bitmapSize, transparentImage, transparencyColor (default 15); byte array[32][32] palette indices [x][y] ; attribs (name[21], 3 type bytes, misc, weight, description[256]). BKG.DAT 19,680 = 15×1312. - Sprite, 9262 B: 8 frames (DOWN½, UP½, LEFT½, RIGHT½) + speed, dimensions, direction, X, Y + temp array + struct time . - Map: 1458 B = unsigned char Map[6][15][15] + 6 exits (old: 2808 B with int ). Exit = name[13] + pad + int X, Y. Layers: background, wall, object, scenery, door. 3. Assets # Asset Where Format 2000 tile art 7_31_00/raw/ , Galimore Archive/Galimore Tiles/ , Galimore Specs/Galimore Tiles/ 32×32 / 16×16 RGB raw 2000 game tiles 7_31_00/bg (25), fg (29), get (2); X/mapedit_Binary/*.dat 2332 B objects ( R/bg.png , R/fg.png , R/get.png ) Maps X/mapedit_Binary/{house,map,test}.map 114,692 B ( R/house_crop.png , R/map_crop.png ) Sprites pockets.spr , Sprite Testing/pockets_*.raw , Galimore Sprites/* .spr , raw, .psd , .gif ( R/pockets.png ) Objects / icons Galimore Objects/* , The 5 Points/* .psd / .psp World design Continent*.psd , Experiment Town.psd , House Example.jpg Photoshop 1999 art X/CU_galisource072399/ (70 bitmaps; sprites JABBA/MONK/MONST/PIMP/DOUG/MAN) 1312 B bitmaps, 9262 B sprites Sound Sound Effects/Stephen King/ (21) Mac resource forks only 4. Code quality and notable points # Good ideas: stable tile IDs (blank instead of delete); size-based type sniffing; Allegro driver trimming; reusable ID-dispatched widget toolkit with a "GUI Shell" starter template; per-function debug gating; Photoshop RAW interop; two-floor maps with a 64-bit per-cell property mask and layer-switch bit; palette-gradient fire for animated tiles; the editor doubles as the renderer. Bugs spotted (reported, not changed): 1. g_map.cpp saveMap() / loadMap() : char *fileName; strcpy(fileName, …) (uninitialized pointer). 2. g_map.cpp drawATile() : uninitialized theTileVector , no default: case. 3. mapeditor_gui.cpp : visibleLayers bit layouts disagree, and init uses && for & . 4. "Transparent" mask checkbox has no handler. 5. GALIMORE_OBJECT::getBitmap() has no return . 6. convertTo15() is identical to convertTo16() . 7. Sprite-frame copy constructor copies only 32×32 of 32×48; displayFrame() size mismatch. 8. Attribute copy/assignment skip objectWeight . 9. ~GALIMORE_BITMAP_OBJECT destroys bitmaps shared by vector copies. 10. g_mask.h constants are unsigned short but shift up to bit 25 (bits ≥ 16 are zero). 11. loadDataFile dedups by pixels, so identical tiles would collapse [inferred risk]. 12. do{}while(infile) processes the failed final read once more. 13. .dat order depends on directory order; memory-dump formats are compiler/endian-specific. Unfinished: no 2000-era game runtime; sprite layer; object attributes; mask replacement tiles; Linux port; script editor, character generation, NPC AI, OpenPlay networking. RPG Tools / Phosphor (Aug 2000): rpg_map.h (map class renamed C_RPGMap ), rpg_raw.h (LGPL), gcc Makefile, a CodeWarrior project (the only real classic-Mac toolchain artefact), CVS at cvs.rpgtools.sourceforge.net , naming style in Text Docs/CODING_STYLE.txt ( C_ classes, S_ structs, g globals, k / gk constants). 5. Relevance to GlitchyGames # Roadmap #11 "Level/room data format (and tilemaps)" is open; each game rolls its own ScreenData / FloorData / LevelManager ( plans/engine-audit.md ). 5.1 Worth porting # Map model for #11: Galimore's ordered layers (bg → fg → objects → actors), per-cell properties kept separate from the art, and named exits with entry points. The GlitchyGames design built from these ideas, adjusted for today's games and constraints (object layers, a typed property vocabulary, exit regions with named spawn points), is plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-a-tilemap-format.md . Stable tile IDs: explicit IDs or tombstones, never list position. Collision on the map cell, separate from the art. Editor features: Mapedit's brush sizes, property-paint mode with pick-up/stamp, layer and floor visibility, tileset palette, eraser = 0; Galibmap's colour wells, frame drag-reorder, and the 9-frame walk-cycle convention. Animated tiles via animation frames, or a procedural fire buffer. 5.2 Converting Galimore data # The survey's read-only decoder (not in this repository) decodes everything below to PNG; sub-plan E ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-e-galimore-import.md ) plans a reviewed converter. - Tiles: <1024H , transpose from [x][y] , RGB565 → RGB888, 0xF81F → magenta; write TOML pixels + [colors] (10–60 colours per tile); keep the 1-based .dat index as the tile ID. - Sprites: 16 × 32×48 frames ( <1536H , [x][y] ); drop all-grey frames; walk_down (0–2), walk_up (3–5), walk_side (6–8, mirrored). - Raw: RGB888 row-major → PNG for Bitmappy. - Maps: offsets in §2.3; layers per floor; mask bits → named properties. - 1999 data: 1312 B indexed bitmaps (palette from GTORAW or GALIMORE PALLETE.GIF ; honour transparencyColor ), 9262 B 8-frame sprites, 1458 / 2808 B maps with exits — the best test case for a room/exit design. - Caveats: tiles may be RGB555 if saved in 15-bit mode; attribute blocks are empty; sounds need resource-fork extraction first (e.g. DeRez ).

docs.text: Sources src/galibmap.cpp , src/bmap_gui.cpp , src/gmore_raw.cpp , src/g_object.cpp , src/g_sprite.cpp ; binary X/bitmap_Binary/galibmap.exe . - Space toggles object mode (8 frames of 32×32) and sprite mode (16 frames of 32×48). - 6× zoomed canvas: left-drag paints, right-drag eyedropper; drag frames in the strip to copy or reorder. - R/G/B sliders, three colour wells (C cycles, R replaces colour 2 with colour 1); New / Save / Load / Quit; keys 1–8, N, L, S, Esc. - Load branches purely on file_size : 2332 → object, 49152 → sprite, 3072 → raw tile, 4608 → raw sprite frame (the file browser filters by the same sizes). GALIMORE_OBJECT (tile/object), 2332 bytes ( .bg , .fg , .get ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 2048 | INT16 array[32][32] , [x][y] (offset (x·32+y)·2), RGB565 ; 0xF81F = transparent | | 2048 | 21 | objectName | | 2069 | 1 | objectType | | 2070 | 1 | objectState | | 2071 | 1 | objectSpecial | | 2072 | 2 | objectIsUsableBy (UINT16) | | 2074 | 1 | objectWeight | | 2075 | 256 | objectDescription | | 2331 | 1 | pad | The attribute block is all zeros in every shipped .dat (never authored). GALIMORE_SPRITE, 49,152 bytes ( .spr ): 16 × short array[32][48] , [x][y] RGB565. Frame plan ( spriteguide.html ): front / away / side × still / walk-R / walk-L, side mirrored → 9 used. pockets.spr uses 6 (rest grey). RAW, 3072 / 4608 bytes ( .raw ): headerless 8-bit RGB, row-major , 32×32 or 32×48 (Photoshop Raw export). Pipeline: Photoshop → .raw → Galibmap → .bg/.fg/.get/.spr .

docs.text: .dat = 2332-byte records back to back (58,300 = 25×2332, 67,628 = 29×2332, 4,664 = 2×2332). Stable tile IDs: maps store 1-based indices; on update Galimake loads the existing .dat , zeros (doesn't delete) records whose pixels no longer match a file , refreshes matches, and puts new tiles in the first blank slot, so map indices never shift.

docs.text: Sources src/mapedit.cpp , src/mapeditor_gui.cpp , src/g_map.cpp , include/g_map.h . - 14×14 map view with scroll bars; 4×6 tile palette; layer tabs Fgnd / Bgnd / Obj / Spr / Mask ; floor radios 1F / 2F with show-layer checkboxes; "Make a Mask" and "Eraser" (tile 0). - Brush sizes 1–4; s / l save / load; Esc quits. - Mask tab: drag to stamp, right-click to pick up; magenta = no mask, purple = current, black = other. - Mask bits: 0 LAYER_SWITCH, 1 UNPASSABLE_GOOD, 2 UNPASSABLE_BAD, 3 UNPASSABLE_NEUTRAL, 4 DEEP, 5 BRIDGE, 6 CHASM, 7 PUSHABLE, 8 TRANSPARENT. An older plan ( g_mask.h , Dec 1999) added exits, burnable/bombable/freezable, hot/cold, anti-magic, death, door, soil, farmed, layer 2; "Mask Cases" planned a replacement tile in the upper 16 bits (e.g. burnt version) — never implemented. GALIMORE_MAP, 114,692 bytes (arrays [floor][x][y] ; verified by decoding house.map ): | Offset | Size | Field | |---|---|---| | 0 | 1 | landscape (always 0) | | 1 | 8192 | UINT8 fgLayer[2][64][64] (N → record N-1 of fg.dat ; 0 = empty) | | 8193 | 8192 | UINT8 bgLayer → bg.dat | | 16385 | 1 | pad | | 16386 | 16384 | UINT16 objectLayer → get.dat | | 32770 | 16384 | UINT16 spriteLayer (unimplemented) | | 49154 | 2 | pad | | 49156 | 65536 | UINT64 maskLayer | 64×64 cells per floor, 2 floors. Samples: house.map (cottage on grass, 14 fg tiles, 1 object, 40 fully-impassable mask cells), map.map (lattice test), test.map (18 cells of tile 1).

Exit = name[13] + pad + int X, Y. Layers: background, wall, object, scenery, door.

docs.title: 3. Assets

docs.text: Good ideas: stable tile IDs (blank instead of delete); size-based type sniffing; Allegro driver trimming; reusable ID-dispatched widget toolkit with a "GUI Shell" starter template; per-function debug gating; Photoshop RAW interop; two-floor maps with a 64-bit per-cell property mask and layer-switch bit; palette-gradient fire for animated tiles; the editor doubles as the renderer. Bugs spotted (reported, not changed): 1. g_map.cpp saveMap() / loadMap() : char *fileName; strcpy(fileName, …) (uninitialized pointer). 2. g_map.cpp drawATile() : uninitialized theTileVector , no default: case. 3. mapeditor_gui.cpp : visibleLayers bit layouts disagree, and init uses && for & . 4. "Transparent" mask checkbox has no handler. 5. GALIMORE_OBJECT::getBitmap() has no return . 6. convertTo15() is identical to convertTo16() . 7. Sprite-frame copy constructor copies only 32×32 of 32×48; displayFrame() size mismatch. 8. Attribute copy/assignment skip objectWeight . 9. ~GALIMORE_BITMAP_OBJECT destroys bitmaps shared by vector copies. 10. g_mask.h constants are unsigned short but shift up to bit 25 (bits ≥ 16 are zero). 11. loadDataFile dedups by pixels, so identical tiles would collapse [inferred risk]. 12. do{}while(infile) processes the failed final read once more. 13. .dat order depends on directory order; memory-dump formats are compiler/endian-specific. Unfinished: no 2000-era game runtime; sprite layer; object attributes; mask replacement tiles; Linux port; script editor, character generation, NPC AI, OpenPlay networking. RPG Tools / Phosphor (Aug 2000): rpg_map.h (map class renamed C_RPGMap ), rpg_raw.h (LGPL), gcc Makefile, a CodeWarrior project (the only real classic-Mac toolchain artefact), CVS at cvs.rpgtools.sourceforge.net , naming style in Text Docs/CODING_STYLE.txt ( C_ classes, S_ structs, g globals, k / gk constants).

docs.title: 5. Relevance to GlitchyGames

docs.text: Map model for #11: Galimore's ordered layers (bg → fg → objects → actors), per-cell properties kept separate from the art, and named exits with entry points. The GlitchyGames design built from these ideas, adjusted for today's games and constraints (object layers, a typed property vocabulary, exit regions with named spawn points), is plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-a-tilemap-format.md . Stable tile IDs: explicit IDs or tombstones, never list position. Collision on the map cell, separate from the art. Editor features: Mapedit's brush sizes, property-paint mode with pick-up/stamp, layer and floor visibility, tileset palette, eraser = 0; Galibmap's colour wells, frame drag-reorder, and the 9-frame walk-cycle convention. Animated tiles via animation frames, or a procedural fire buffer.
docs.title: 5.1 Worth porting

docs.text: The survey's read-only decoder (not in this repository) decodes everything below to PNG; sub-plan E ( plans/2026-10-18-level-tools-e-galimore-import.md ) plans a reviewed converter. - Tiles: <1024H , transpose from [x][y] , RGB565 → RGB888, 0xF81F → magenta; write TOML pixels + [colors] (10–60 colours per tile); keep the 1-based .dat index as the tile ID. - Sprites: 16 × 32×48 frames ( <1536H , [x][y] ); drop all-grey frames; walk_down (0–2), walk_up (3–5), walk_side (6–8, mirrored). - Raw: RGB888 row-major → PNG for Bitmappy. - Maps: offsets in §2.3; layers per floor; mask bits → named properties. - 1999 data: 1312 B indexed bitmaps (palette from GTORAW or GALIMORE PALLETE.GIF ; honour transparencyColor ), 9262 B 8-frame sprites, 1458 / 2808 B maps with exits — the best test case for a room/exit design. - Caveats: tiles may be RGB555 if saved in 15-bit mode; attribute blocks are empty; sounds need resource-fork extraction first (e.g. DeRez ).

docs.text: Multi-Controller System Documentation # Overview # The Multi-Controller System enables up to 4 simultaneous controllers to navigate and interact with the bitmappy tool independently. Each controller has its own visual indicator, navigation state, and can operate simultaneously without conflicts. Features # Multi-Controller Support : Up to 4 simultaneous controllers Independent Navigation : Each controller navigates film strips and frames independently Visual Distinction : A unique color for each controller (Red, Green, Blue, Yellow): triangles on the film strips, squares on the canvas, circles on the sliders Smart Positioning : Automatic collision avoidance when multiple controllers select the same spot State Preservation : Controllers maintain their selection state when switching between them Hotplug Support : Controllers can be connected/disconnected during operation Architecture # Core Components # MultiControllerManager ( glitchygames/bitmappy/controllers/manager.py ) - Central singleton managing all controllers ControllerSelection ( glitchygames/bitmappy/controllers/selection.py ) - Individual controller state management VisualCollisionManager ( glitchygames/bitmappy/indicators/collision.py ) - Smart positioning and collision avoidance ModeSwitcher ( glitchygames/bitmappy/controllers/modes.py ) - Each controller's mode (film strip, canvas, R/G/B slider), switched with the L2/R2 triggers Integration with Bitmappy - ControllerEventHandler ( glitchygames/bitmappy/controllers/event_handler.py ) and the per-mode button strategies ( glitchygames/bitmappy/controllers/strategies.py ) The button and trigger bindings are listed in CONTROLLER_CONTROLS_README.md at the repository root. Controller Color Scheme # MultiControllerManager.CONTROLLER_COLORS , indexed by controller ID. In Bitmappy, activating a controller (Start) gives it the next color in activation order ( assign_color_to_controller ), so the first controller activated is red: Controller 0 : Red (255, 0, 0) Controller 1 : Green (0, 255, 0) Controller 2 : Blue (0, 0, 255) Controller 3 : Yellow (255, 255, 0) Usage Examples # Basic Setup # from glitchygames.bitmappy.controllers import ControllerSelection , MultiControllerManager from glitchygames.bitmappy.indicators import VisualCollisionManager # Initialize the system (MultiControllerManager is a singleton) manager = MultiControllerManager () visual_manager = VisualCollisionManager () controller_selections = {} # Find the connected controllers (through the engine's devices door; at most once a second) connected_instance_ids = manager . scan_for_controllers () # Set up a controller: only a connected controller can be assigned (None otherwise) instance_id = connected_instance_ids [ 0 ] controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) Controller Activation # # Activate a controller controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () manager . activate_controller ( instance_id ) # Set initial selection controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "animation_name" , 0 ) # Add visual indicator visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = controller_id , instance_id = instance_id , color = manager . CONTROLLER_COLORS [ controller_id ], position = ( 100 , 100 ) ) Navigation # # Navigate to different animation/frame controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "new_animation" , 5 ) # Get current selection animation , frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () print ( f "Controller { controller_id } is at { animation } , frame { frame } " ) # Get navigation history (an entry is added when the animation changes) history = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_navigation_history () for entry in history : print ( f "Previous: { entry [ 'animation' ] } , frame { entry [ 'frame' ] } " ) Multi-Controller Navigation # # Set up multiple controllers for i , instance_id in enumerate ( manager . scan_for_controllers ()): controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () # Each controller can navigate independently controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( f "animation_ { i } " , i ) # Add visual indicators visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = controller_id , instance_id = instance_id , color = manager . CONTROLLER_COLORS [ controller_id ], position = ( 100 + i * 50 , 100 ) ) # All controllers can navigate independently controller_selections [ 0 ] . set_selection ( "animation_A" , 0 ) controller_selections [ 1 ] . set_selection ( "animation_B" , 1 ) controller_selections [ 2 ] . set_selection ( "animation_C" , 2 ) controller_selections [ 3 ] . set_selection ( "animation_D" , 3 ) Visual Collision Avoidance # # Multiple controllers at same position for i in range ( 3 ): visual_manager . add_controller_indicator ( controller_id = i , instance_id = i , color = ( 255 , 0 , 0 ), position = ( 100 , 100 ) # Same position ) # System automatically applies offsets (VisualCollisionManager.POSITION_PATTERNS) to prevent overlap visual_manager . get_final_position ( 0 ) # (100, 100) - no offset visual_manager . get_final_position ( 1 ) # (85, 85) - (-15, -15) offset visual_manager . get_final_position ( 2 ) # (115, 85) - (15, -15) offset Controller State Management # # Check controller status if manager . is_controller_active ( instance_id ): print ( f "Controller { instance_id } is active" ) # Get controller information info = manager . get_controller_info ( instance_id ) if info : print ( f "Controller { info . controller_id } : { info . status . value } " ) # Deactivate controller (the manager has no deactivate; cleanup_inactive_controllers() # unassigns controllers idle for more than ASSIGNMENT_TIMEOUT seconds) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . deactivate () Hotplug Support # # Handle controller connection def on_controller_connected ( instance_id ): controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) print ( f "Controller { controller_id } connected" ) # Handle controller disconnection def on_controller_disconnected ( instance_id ): if instance_id in manager . assigned_controllers : controller_id = manager . assigned_controllers [ instance_id ] if controller_id in controller_selections : del controller_selections [ controller_id ] print ( f "Controller { controller_id } disconnected" ) Integration with Bitmappy # Event Handling # Bitmappy's ControllerEventHandler.on_controller_button_down_event scans for controllers, assigns the controller on its first button press, and passes the button to its current mode's strategy ( FilmStripModeStrategy , CanvasModeStrategy or SliderModeStrategy ). A simplified version of the film strip navigation: def on_controller_button_down_event ( event ): """Handle controller button presses in bitmappy.""" controller_id = manager . get_controller_id ( event . instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : if event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START : # Start button - activate the controller on the first frame of the first animation if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "first_animation" , 0 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT : # D-pad left - previous frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () if current_frame > 0 : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame - 1 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT : # D-pad right - next frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame + 1 ) Film Strip Integration # def update_film_strip_indicators (): """Update visual indicators on film strips.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () # Update visual indicator position if animation in film_strips : # frame_layouts maps (animation, frame) to the frame's rect on the strip frame_rect = film_strips [ animation ] . frame_layouts [ animation , frame ] visual_manager . update_controller_position ( controller_id , frame_rect . midtop ) Advanced Features # State Cloning # # Clone controller state to another controller source_controller = controller_selections [ 0 ] target_controller = controller_selections [ 1 ] source_controller . set_selection ( "animation_A" , 5 ) source_controller . clone_state_to ( target_controller ) # Target controller now has same state animation , frame = target_controller . get_selection () assert animation == "animation_A" assert frame == 5 Navigation History # # Track navigation history controller = controller_selections [ 0 ] controller . set_selection ( "animation1" , 0 ) controller . set_selection ( "animation2" , 1 ) controller . set_selection ( "animation3" , 2 ) # Get history history = controller . get_navigation_history () print ( f "Navigation history: { len ( history ) } entries" ) for entry in history : print ( f " { entry [ 'animation' ] } , frame { entry [ 'frame' ] } " ) Performance Optimization # # Clean up inactive controllers manager . cleanup_inactive_controllers () # Optimize visual positioning visual_manager . optimize_positioning () # Clear all indicators visual_manager . clear_all_indicators () Error Handling # Invalid Operations # # Handle invalid controller IDs gracefully if not manager . is_controller_active ( 999 ): print ( "Controller 999 not found" ) # Handle missing controller selections if controller_id not in controller_selections : print ( f "Controller { controller_id } not initialized" ) System Resilience # # System handles rapid controller switching for cycle in range ( 1000 ): for i in range ( 4 ): if i in controller_selections : controller_selections [ i ] . set_selection ( f "animation_ { i } " , cycle % 50 ) # System handles controller disconnection/reconnection for i in range ( 10 ): manager . _handle_controller_connect ( i ) # ... use controller ... manager . _handle_controller_disconnect ( i ) Best Practices # 1. Controller Lifecycle Management # def setup_controller ( instance_id ): """Properly set up a new controller.""" controller_id = manager . assign_controller ( instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : controller_selections [ controller_id ] = ControllerSelection ( controller_id , instance_id ) controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () manager . activate_controller ( instance_id ) return controller_id return None def cleanup_controller ( instance_id ): """Properly clean up a controller.""" if instance_id in manager . assigned_controllers : controller_id = manager . assigned_controllers [ instance_id ] if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . deactivate () del controller_selections [ controller_id ] 2. Visual Indicator Management # def update_controller_visuals (): """Update all controller visual indicators.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () position = get_frame_position ( animation , frame ) visual_manager . update_controller_position ( controller_id , position ) 3. State Synchronization # def sync_controller_states (): """Synchronize controller states with UI.""" for controller_id , selection in controller_selections . items (): if selection . is_active (): animation , frame = selection . get_selection () # Update UI elements update_film_strip_selection ( controller_id , animation , frame ) update_visual_indicator ( controller_id , animation , frame ) Troubleshooting # Common Issues # Controller not responding Check if controller is assigned: manager.assigned_controllers Verify controller is active: manager.is_controller_active(instance_id) Visual indicators overlapping System automatically handles collision avoidance Check collision groups: visual_manager.film_strip_collision_groups , canvas_collision_groups or slider_collision_groups State not preserved Ensure controller selection is activated: selection.activate() Check navigation history: selection.get_navigation_history() Debug Information # # Get system status print ( f "Active controllers: { manager . get_active_controllers () } " ) print ( f "Visual indicators: { len ( visual_manager . indicators ) } " ) print ( f "Collision summary: { visual_manager . get_collision_summary () } " ) # Get controller details for instance_id , info in manager . controllers . items (): print ( f "Controller { info . controller_id } : { info . status . value } , color { info . color } " ) Future Extensions # The multi-controller system provides a foundation for: Collaborative Editing : Multiple users editing simultaneously Advanced Visual Management : Custom indicators and positioning Session Management : Save/load controller configurations Permission Systems : Master/slave controller relationships API Reference # MultiControllerManager # scan_for_controllers() - Scan for connected controllers (at most once per scan_interval , 1 s) and return their instance IDs assign_controller(instance_id) - Assign a controller ID to a connected controller activate_controller(instance_id) - Activate an assigned controller assign_color_to_controller(controller_id) - Give a controller the next color in activation order get_controller_id(instance_id) / get_controller_color(instance_id) - Look up an assigned controller is_controller_active(instance_id) - Check if controller is active get_controller_info(instance_id) - Get controller information get_active_controllers() - Get list of active controllers cleanup_inactive_controllers() - Unassign controllers idle for more than ASSIGNMENT_TIMEOUT (5 s) ControllerSelection # activate() - Activate the controller deactivate() - Deactivate the controller set_selection(animation, frame) - Set animation and frame get_selection() - Get current animation and frame get_navigation_history() - Get navigation history clone_state_to(other) - Clone state to another controller VisualCollisionManager # add_controller_indicator(controller_id, instance_id, color, position, location_type=LocationType.FILM_STRIP) - Add visual indicator (a triangle on the film strip, a square on the canvas, a circle on a slider) remove_controller_indicator(controller_id) - Remove visual indicator update_controller_position(controller_id, position) - Update indicator position get_final_position(controller_id) - Get final position with offsets optimize_positioning() - Optimize all indicator positions clear_all_indicators() - Remove every indicator

A simplified version of the film strip navigation: def on_controller_button_down_event ( event ): """Handle controller button presses in bitmappy.""" controller_id = manager . get_controller_id ( event . instance_id ) if controller_id is not None : if event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_START : # Start button - activate the controller on the first frame of the first animation if controller_id in controller_selections : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . activate () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( "first_animation" , 0 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_LEFT : # D-pad left - previous frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () if current_frame > 0 : controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame - 1 ) elif event . button == pygame . CONTROLLER_BUTTON_DPAD_RIGHT : # D-pad right - next frame if controller_id in controller_selections : current_animation , current_frame = controller_selections [ controller_id ] . get_selection () controller_selections [ controller_id ] . set_selection ( current_animation , current_frame + 1 )

Command-Line Argument System # GlitchyGames uses a composable argparse architecture where the engine, event managers, font system, and individual games each contribute argument groups to a single parser. Every game built on the engine automatically inherits all engine-level flags, and can extend the parser with its own game-specific options. How Arguments Are Assembled # The orchestration happens in GameEngine.initialize_arguments() , called from GameEngine.__init__() . The flow is: sequenceDiagram participant GE as GameEngine.__init__() participant IA as initialize_arguments(game_class) participant AP as ArgumentParser participant ENGINE as GameEngine.args() participant MGR as Event Manager .args() x12 participant GAME as game_class.args() participant NS as Namespace GE->>IA: initialize_arguments(game_class) IA->>AP: ArgumentParser("GameName version X.Y") IA->>ENGINE: GameEngine.args(parser) Note over ENGINE: Adds "Graphics Options" group
15 arguments,
and "Diagnostics Options"
16 arguments (2 hidden:
replay restart internals) ENGINE->>MGR: AppEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "App Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: AudioEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Sound Mixer Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: ControllerEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Controller Options" group
1 argument ENGINE->>MGR: DropEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Drop Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: FontManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Font Options" group
7 arguments ENGINE->>MGR: GameEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Game Options" group
3 arguments ENGINE->>MGR: JoystickEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Joystick Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: KeyboardEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Keyboard Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: MidiEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Midi Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: MouseEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Mouse Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: TouchEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Touch Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE->>MGR: WindowEventManager.args(parser) Note over MGR: Adds "Window Options" group
(empty, reserved) ENGINE-->>IA: return parser IA->>AP: parser.add_argument_group("GameName vX.Y Options") IA->>GAME: game_class.args(game_group) Note over GAME: Adds game-specific arguments
to its own group IA->>AP: parser.parse_args() AP-->>NS: Namespace with all arguments IA->>IA: GameEngine.OPTIONS = vars(args) IA->>IA: Derive synthetic: debug_events IA->>IA: Back-propagate: game.options = OPTIONS The Argument Group Hierarchy # Each layer adds its own add_argument_group() , producing clearly separated sections in --help output. The hierarchy mirrors the engine architecture. flowchart TD subgraph Parser["ArgumentParser: GameName version X.Y"] subgraph L1["Layer 1: Graphics Options (GameEngine)"] F1["-f, --target-fps"] F2["--fps-log-interval-ms"] F3["-w, --windowed"] F4["-r, --resolution"] F5["--use-gfxdraw"] F6["--update-type"] F7["--timer-backend"] F8["--sleep-granularity-ns"] F9["--windows-timer-1ms"] F16["--random-seed"] F17["--screen-shake-intensity, --rumble-intensity"] F18["--live-voice-pool"] F20["--default-background"] F19["--video-driver"] end subgraph L1D["Layer 1: Diagnostics Options (GameEngine)"] D1["--log-timer-jitter, --perf-trim-percent, --fps-histogram"] D2["--debug-overlay"] D3["--record-trace, --replay-trace, --replay-fps"] D4["--audit, --replay-digest, --replay-pause-at-frame"] D6["--compare-processing, --max-processing-slowdown, --rebaseline"] D5["--headless"] end subgraph L2["Layer 2: Event Manager Groups"] subgraph AO["App Options"] AO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph SM["Sound Mixer Options"] SM_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph DO["Drop Options"] DO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph CO["Controller Options"] CO1["--input-mode"] end subgraph FO["Font Options"] FO1["--font-name"] FO2["--font-size"] FO3["--font-bold"] FO4["--font-italic"] FO5["--font-antialias"] FO6["--font-dpi"] FO7["--font-system"] end subgraph GO["Game Options"] GO1["-l, --log-level"] GO2["--no-unhandled-events"] GO3["-p, --profile"] end subgraph JO["Joystick Options"] JO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph KO["Keyboard Options"] KO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph MIO["Midi Options"] MIO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph MO["Mouse Options"] MO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph TO["Touch Options"] TO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end subgraph WO["Window Options"] WO_EMPTY["(no arguments yet)"] end end subgraph L3["Layer 3: Game-Specific Options"] GS["(varies per game)"] end end How Games Add Arguments # A game adds arguments by defining a @classmethod called args() on its scene class. The engine discovers this method via getattr(game, 'args', None) and calls it with a dedicated argument group. If the game does not define args() , the engine logs an informational message and continues. flowchart TD subgraph Engine["GameEngine.initialize_arguments()"] CHECK{"getattr(game, 'args', None)"} CHECK -->|"method exists"| GROUP["parser.add_argument_group( GameName vX.Y Options)"] GROUP --> CALL["game.args(group)"] CHECK -->|"None"| LOG["log.info: Game does not implement arguments"] end subgraph GameCode["Your Game Scene"] ARGS["@classmethod def args(cls, parser): parser.add_argument(...)"] end CALL --> ARGS Pattern: Minimal Game # class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) Pattern: Game with Custom Options # class TimedDemo ( Scene ): NAME = 'Timed Demo' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): parser . add_argument ( '--time' , type = int , default = 10 , help = 'time in seconds to wait before quitting' , ) parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) Note that the game receives an argument group , not the root parser. This means game arguments appear under their own heading in --help output. OPTIONS Dictionary Flow # After parsing, the Namespace is converted to a plain dict and propagated to every component that needs it. flowchart TD PARSE["parser.parse_args()"] --> VARS["vars(args) Namespace -> dict"] VARS --> OPT["GameEngine.OPTIONS (class var)"] OPT --> SYNTH{"log_level in DEBUG/CRITICAL/ERROR?"} SYNTH -->|"Yes"| DEBUG_T["OPTIONS['debug_events'] = True"] SYNTH -->|"No"| DEBUG_F["OPTIONS['debug_events'] = False"] DEBUG_T & DEBUG_F --> BACKPROP["game.options = OPTIONS"] BACKPROP --> SM_OPT["SceneManager.OPTIONS = OPTIONS"] SM_OPT --> SCENE_INIT["Scene.__init__(options=OPTIONS)"] SCENE_INIT --> SELF_OPT["self.options = OPTIONS"] subgraph Access["Runtime Access"] A1["self.options['target_fps']"] A2["self.options['font_name']"] A3["self.options['log_level']"] A4["self.options['debug_events']"] A5["GameEngine.OPTIONS['resolution']"] end SELF_OPT --> Access Complete Flag Reference # Graphics Options # Added by GameEngine.args() in glitchygames/engine/game_engine.py . Flag Type Default Description -f , --target-fps float None (the game's TARGET_FPS , else 60.01) Cap the framerate; 0 = uncapped --fps-log-interval-ms float 1000 How often to log the FPS counter in ms -w , --windowed store_true True Run in windowed mode (the default is already True , so the flag changes nothing) -r , --resolution str 800x480 Display resolution (WxH) --use-gfxdraw store_true False Use pygame.gfxdraw for rendering --update-type choice update Display update method: update or flip --timer-backend choice auto Timer backend: auto (the fast backend with this machine's sleep delay measured, so each sleep wakes in time), fast (assumes sleeps wake on time) or pygame (legacy) --sleep-granularity-ns int 1000000 How long before each frame deadline the fast backend is to wake from its sleep and spin (ns); 0 spins only --windows-timer-1ms store_true False On Windows, request 1ms system timer resolution --video-driver choice None Platform-specific video driver (see below) --random-seed int random 64-bit Master seed for every engine random stream --screen-shake-intensity float 1.0 Screen shake strength, 0.0 (off) to 1.0 --rumble-intensity float 1.0 Controller rumble strength, 0.0 (off) to 1.0 --live-voice-pool int 4 Mixer channels reserved for real-time synth voices --default-background choice test-pattern Background of a scene that sets none: test-pattern (the TV test pattern) or channel-3 (the channel 3 blue screen) --video-driver choices by platform: Platform Choices Linux wayland , x11 , dga , fbcon , directfb , ggi , vgl , svgalib , aalib Windows windib , directx macOS (none currently defined; the code checks platform.system() == 'MacOS' , which never matches, so macOS falls through to no choices either way) Diagnostics Options # Added by GameEngine.args() right after the Graphics Options: how any run is watched, recorded, replayed or diagnosed, whatever the game. They change no game settings. Flag Type Default Description --log-timer-jitter store_true False Log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically --perf-trim-percent float 5.0 Percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in FPS report --fps-histogram choice equal-range FPS histogram buckets in the shutdown report: equal-range or target-relative --debug-overlay / --no-debug-overlay bool False Show the debug overlay at startup (F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels) --record-trace PATH None Record the session to a gzip JSON Lines trace ( Gameplay Recording and Replay ) --replay-trace PATH None Replay a recording exactly, reporting the first divergence --replay-fps choice None (read as recorded ) With --replay-trace : FPS events from the recorded or the real frame times --audit / --no-audit bool False With --replay-trace : replay twice in fresh processes and compare (exit 0, 3 when nondeterministic, 70 when a run could not finish; see exit codes ) --replay-digest PATH None With --replay-trace : write a SHA-256 per replayed frame (used by --audit ) --compare-processing store_true False With --replay-trace --headless : report how each frame's processing time compares with the recording's --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT None With --replay-trace --headless (implies --compare-processing ): exit 8 when a matched replay took more than PERCENT longer --rebaseline NEW None With --replay-trace OLD --headless : replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences and write the run's recording to NEW --replay-pause-at-frame N (non-negative int) None With --replay-trace , watched: skip the start screen, rebuild frames 0 to N - 1 unpresented, then pause with frame N next (what step back restarts with; ignored with --headless ; step back ) --headless store_true False Run on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers (no window, no sound); a replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout ( headless runs ) Game Options # Added by GameEventManager.args() in glitchygames/events/game.py . Flag Type Default Description -l , --log-level choice info Logging level: debug , info , warning , error , critical --no-unhandled-events store_true False Raise UnhandledEventError on unhandled events -p , --profile store_true False Enable cProfile profiling Controller Options # Added by ControllerEventManager.args() in glitchygames/events/controller.py . Flag Type Default Description --input-mode choice auto Which gamepads the game sees: auto (every device; a mapped pad sends controller events, any other device joystick events), joystick (every device sends joystick events) or controller (mapped pads only). See Event System Font Options # Added by FontManager.args() in glitchygames/fonts/font_manager.py . Flag Type Default Description --font-name str Vera Font name: the bundled Vera , VeraBd , VeraIt or VeraBI ; any other name is looked up among the system's fonts --font-size int 14 Font size in points --font-bold store_true False Bold font --font-italic store_true False Italic font --font-antialias store_true False Enable font antialiasing --font-dpi int 72 Font DPI --font-system choice freetype Font system: freetype (enhanced) or pygame (built-in) Reserved Groups (Empty, No Arguments Yet) # These groups exist as extension points. Each event manager creates its argument group but does not currently populate it with any flags. Group Name Source File Manager Class App Options events/app.py AppEventManager Sound Mixer Options events/audio.py AudioEventManager Drop Options events/drop.py DropEventManager Joystick Options events/joystick.py JoystickEventManager Keyboard Options events/keyboard.py KeyboardEventManager Midi Options events/midi.py MidiEventManager Mouse Options events/mouse.py MouseEventManager Touch Options events/touch.py TouchEventManager Window Options events/window.py WindowEventManager Synthetic Options (Not from argparse) # These are derived after parsing and injected into the OPTIONS dict. Key Type Derived From Description debug_events bool log_level Meant to be True for the debug , critical and error levels, but the code compares with upper-case names while --log-level is lower case, so it is always False (BUGS.md #74) Bitmappy Game-Specific Arguments # Added by BitmapEditorScene.args() in glitchygames/bitmappy/editor.py . These appear under the heading "Bitmappy vX.Y Options" in --help . Flag Type Default Description -v , --version store_true False Print the game version and exit -s , --size str 32x32 Canvas size (WxH in pixels) Example Game Arguments # Other games in the project demonstrate the pattern: Game File Arguments Paddle Slap glitchygames/examples/paddleslap.py -v, --version , -b, --balls (int, default 1), --ball-spawn-mode (choice, default paddle_only ) DT Demo glitchygames/examples/dt_demo.py -v, --version , -b, --balls (int, default 1) Clockwork Keep glitchygames/examples/clockwork_keep/game.py --floor (int, default 0) Brave Adventurer (both editions) glitchygames/examples/brave_adventurer/game.py , glitchygames/examples/brave_adventurer_papyrus/game.py -v, --version Joystick Demo glitchygames/examples/joystick_demo.py none (the engine's --input-mode chooses what it shows) Bitrot Adventures scripts/bitrotadventures.py -s, --some-game-specific-option Animation Demo scripts/animation_scene_full_demo.py -v, --version What --help Looks Like # When a user runs uv run bitmappy --help , argparse produces output structured like this (argument groups appear in registration order; argparse leaves out groups with no arguments, such as App Options): usage: Bitmappy version X.Y [-h] [-f TARGET_FPS] [...] options: -h, --help show this help message and exit Graphics Options: -f, --target-fps cap the framerate (default: the game's TARGET_FPS, else 60.01; 0 = uncapped) --fps-log-interval-ms how often to log the FPS counter in ms (default: 1000) -w, --windowed run the program in windowed mode -r, --resolution the resolution to use (default: 1024x768) --use-gfxdraw --update-type update or flip (default: update) --timer-backend timer backend for draw loop pacing (default: auto, the fast backend with this machine's sleep delay measured, so each sleep wakes in time; fast assumes sleeps wake on time; pygame is the legacy backend) --sleep-granularity-ns how long before each frame deadline the fast backend is to wake from its sleep and spin (ns); 0 spins only --windows-timer-1ms on Windows, request 1ms system timer resolution --random-seed master seed for every engine random stream (...) --screen-shake-intensity, --rumble-intensity, --live-voice-pool --default-background the background of a scene that sets none (...) --video-driver Diagnostics Options: --log-timer-jitter log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically --perf-trim-percent percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in global FPS report --fps-histogram FPS histogram buckets in the shutdown report (...) --debug-overlay, --no-debug-overlay show the debug overlay at startup (F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels) --record-trace PATH record the session (...) --replay-trace PATH replay a --record-trace recording exactly (...) --replay-fps, --audit, --no-audit, --compare-processing, --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT, --replay-pause-at-frame N, --rebaseline NEW, --replay-digest PATH (replay options) --headless run on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers: no window, no sound (...) Controller Options: --input-mode Which gamepads the game sees (default: auto, ...) Font Options: --font-name Font to use (default: the bundled Vera; ...) --font-size --font-bold --font-italic --font-antialias --font-dpi --font-system Font system to use: freetype (enhanced, default) or pygame (built-in) Game Options: -l, --log-level set the logging level --no-unhandled-events fail on unhandled events -p, --profile enable profiling Bitmappy vX.Y Options: -v, --version print the game version and exit -s, --size The --resolution help text says 1024x768, but the default is 800x480 (BUGS.md #76). How to Add Arguments to a New Event Manager # If you are adding arguments to a currently-empty event manager group, follow the existing pattern: # In glitchygames/events/mouse.py @classmethod def args ( cls , parser : argparse . ArgumentParser ) -> argparse . ArgumentParser : group = parser . add_argument_group ( 'Mouse Options' ) group . add_argument ( '--mouse-sensitivity' , type = float , default = 1.0 , help = 'Mouse sensitivity multiplier (default: 1.0)' , ) return parser The engine already calls your manager's args() method — you just need to add add_argument() calls to the existing group. How to Create a New Game with Arguments # from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): """Add game-specific arguments. Args: parser: An argument group (not the root parser). """ parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) parser . add_argument ( '--difficulty' , choices = [ 'easy' , 'medium' , 'hard' ], default = 'medium' , help = 'game difficulty level' , ) def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options ) # Access your arguments via self.options self . difficulty = self . options [ 'difficulty' ] def main (): GameEngine ( game = MyGame ) . start () Your arguments will automatically appear under "My Game v1.0 Options" in the --help output, separate from all engine-level flags.

docs.text: Added by GameEngine.args() right after the Graphics Options: how any run is watched, recorded, replayed or diagnosed, whatever the game. They change no game settings. Flag Type Default Description --log-timer-jitter store_true False Log frame pacing jitter statistics periodically --perf-trim-percent float 5.0 Percent of frames to trim from top and bottom in FPS report --fps-histogram choice equal-range FPS histogram buckets in the shutdown report: equal-range or target-relative --debug-overlay / --no-debug-overlay bool False Show the debug overlay at startup (F3 toggles, F4 cycles panels) --record-trace PATH None Record the session to a gzip JSON Lines trace ( Gameplay Recording and Replay ) --replay-trace PATH None Replay a recording exactly, reporting the first divergence --replay-fps choice None (read as recorded ) With --replay-trace : FPS events from the recorded or the real frame times --audit / --no-audit bool False With --replay-trace : replay twice in fresh processes and compare (exit 0, 3 when nondeterministic, 70 when a run could not finish; see exit codes ) --replay-digest PATH None With --replay-trace : write a SHA-256 per replayed frame (used by --audit ) --compare-processing store_true False With --replay-trace --headless : report how each frame's processing time compares with the recording's --max-processing-slowdown PERCENT None With --replay-trace --headless (implies --compare-processing ): exit 8 when a matched replay took more than PERCENT longer --rebaseline NEW None With --replay-trace OLD --headless : replay OLD on the current code without stopping at divergences and write the run's recording to NEW --replay-pause-at-frame N (non-negative int) None With --replay-trace , watched: skip the start screen, rebuild frames 0 to N - 1 unpresented, then pause with frame N next (what step back restarts with; ignored with --headless ; step back ) --headless store_true False Run on SDL's dummy video and audio drivers (no window, no sound); a replay also runs unpaced and prints its report to stdout ( headless runs )

docs.text: from glitchygames.engine import GameEngine from glitchygames.scenes import Scene class MyGame ( Scene ): NAME = 'My Game' VERSION = '1.0' @classmethod def args ( cls , parser ): """Add game-specific arguments. Args: parser: An argument group (not the root parser). """ parser . add_argument ( '-v' , '--version' , action = 'store_true' , help = 'print the game version and exit' , ) parser . add_argument ( '--difficulty' , choices = [ 'easy' , 'medium' , 'hard' ], default = 'medium' , help = 'game difficulty level' , ) def __init__ ( self , options ): super () . __init__ ( options = options ) # Access your arguments via self.options self . difficulty = self . options [ 'difficulty' ] def main (): GameEngine ( game = MyGame ) . start () Your arguments will automatically appear under "My Game v1.0 Options" in the --help output, separate from all engine-level flags.

Bitmappy Architecture # Bitmappy is GlitchyGames' pixel art editor. These diagrams show how it is wired up through the engine, from bootstrap to rendering. Bootstrap & Main Loop # How Bitmappy starts up: entry point through main() , GameEngine initialization, scene setup, and the main loop (one frame per pass, ended by _finish_frame ). sequenceDiagram participant User participant main as main() participant GE as GameEngine participant SM as SceneManager (singleton) participant BES as BitmapEditorScene User->>main: uv run bitmappy main->>GE: GameEngine(game=BitmapEditorScene, icon=...) GE->>GE: parse CLI args (GameEngine.args() + BitmapEditorScene.args()) GE->>GE: pygame.init(), create display main->>main: load_ai_training_data() main->>GE: engine.start() GE->>BES: BitmapEditorScene(options=OPTIONS) BES->>BES: EditorSetup.init_undo_redo_system() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_menu_bar() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_canvas(options) BES->>BES: SliderManager.setup_sliders_and_color_well() BES->>BES: EditorSetup.setup_debug_text_box() BES->>BES: FilmStripCoordinator.setup_film_strips() GE->>GE: _initialize_event_managers() GE->>SM: scene_manager.switch_to_scene(game) SM->>BES: setup() (AIManager.setup() starts the AI worker) GE->>SM: scene_manager.start() loop Main Game Loop (while active_scene is not None) Note over SM: dt = the previous frame's start-to-start time SM->>SM: camera.begin_frame() SM->>BES: _update_scene() (Scene.dt_tick: logic and collision) SM->>GE: _process_events() GE->>GE: _pump_events() (active_sources().pump_events(): live, pygame.event.get()) GE->>SM: EVENT_HANDLERS[event.type](event) SM->>BES: on_*_event(event) SM->>SM: _run_supervisor_slot() (supervisors, e.g. a recording's) SM->>SM: _update_frame_services() (shake, rumble) SM->>SM: _aim_active_camera() (camera_target / follow) SM->>SM: _position_active_world_sprites() (world sprites' rect, culling) SM->>SM: _render_scene() (BitmapEditorScene.update: animation, controllers, AI, then draw) SM->>SM: _advance_still_camera_shake() (WORLD shake nothing advanced) SM->>SM: _present_frame() (overlay, display update) SM->>SM: _finish_frame() (pace, then set dt once from perf_counter) end Class Hierarchy # Event dispatch chain (how events reach your scene) # EventManager is the base class for GameEngine and SceneManager . Every Scene instead inherits AllEventStubs , which gives it a default on_*_event() method for every event, so events flow through all of them using the same on_*_event() API. Inheritance: flowchart LR EM["EventManager"] --- GE["GameEngine"] EM --- SM["SceneManager"] STUBS["AllEventStubs"] --- SC["Scene"] SC --- BES["BitmapEditorScene"] Event flow — how an SDL event reaches your handler in Bitmappy: flowchart TD SDL["SDL Event"] --> GE["GameEngine
O#40;1#41; EVENT_HANDLERS lookup"] GE --> MGR["Event Manager
e.g. MouseEventManager"] MGR -->|"updates state,
synthesizes events"| SM["SceneManager
forwards to active_scene"] SM --> BES["BitmapEditorScene
#40;the active scene#41;"] BES --> HANDLER["Your handler runs
on_left_mouse_drag_event#40;#41;"] BES --> STUB["No handler?
The stub calls unhandled_event#40;#41;"] The GameEngine receives every SDL event and does an O(1) dict lookup to find the right event manager. The event manager updates its internal state (button tracking, axis values, drag detection) and may synthesize higher-level events (drag, drop, chord). It then forwards to the SceneManager , which passes everything to the active_scene . In Bitmappy, that's BitmapEditorScene , which overrides handlers like on_key_down_event() , on_left_mouse_button_down_event() , on_left_mouse_drag_event() , and on_controller_button_down_event() . Events it doesn't override hit the stubs, which call unhandled_event() : it does nothing by default, logs each event type once when the log level is DEBUG, ERROR or CRITICAL, and raises UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events (as the tests run). EventManager is the base class for GameEngine and SceneManager . Every Scene instead inherits AllEventStubs , which gives it a default on_*_event() method for every event, so events flow through all of them using the same on_*_event() API. Inheritance: flowchart LR EM["EventManager"] --- GE["GameEngine"] EM --- SM["SceneManager"] STUBS["AllEventStubs"] --- SC["Scene"] SC --- BES["BitmapEditorScene"] Event flow — how an SDL event reaches your handler in Bitmappy: flowchart TD SDL["SDL Event"] --> GE["GameEngine
O#40;1#41; EVENT_HANDLERS lookup"] GE --> MGR["Event Manager
e.g. MouseEventManager"] MGR -->|"updates state,
synthesizes events"| SM["SceneManager
forwards to active_scene"] SM --> BES["BitmapEditorScene
#40;the active scene#41;"] BES --> HANDLER["Your handler runs
on_left_mouse_drag_event#40;#41;"] BES --> STUB["No handler?
The stub calls unhandled_event#40;#41;"] The GameEngine receives every SDL event and does an O(1) dict lookup to find the right event manager. The event manager updates its internal state (button tracking, axis values, drag detection) and may synthesize higher-level events (drag, drop, chord). It then forwards to the SceneManager , which passes everything to the active_scene . In Bitmappy, that's BitmapEditorScene , which overrides handlers like on_key_down_event() , on_left_mouse_button_down_event() , on_left_mouse_drag_event() , and on_controller_button_down_event() . Events it doesn't override hit the stubs, which call unhandled_event() : it does nothing by default, logs each event type once when the log level is DEBUG, ERROR or CRITICAL, and raises UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events (as the tests run).

docs.text:
Event System Architecture # GlitchyGames makes it easy to port simple pygame projects into more advanced games with little effort. If you already have a pygame game using pygame.event.get() and if/elif chains, you can bring it into GlitchyGames and immediately benefit from named event handlers, automatic state tracking, and synthesized higher-level events — without rewriting your existing event logic. Porting can be incremental: a scene that defines process_event(event) receives every raw pygame.event.Event from the engine, in order, instead of the on_*_event() callbacks ( GameEngine.process_events ), so an existing if/elif loop body moves in as it is. Adopt the GlitchyGames handlers one event at a time as you need their benefits. Don't call pygame.event.get() yourself: the engine reads SDL's queue once per frame, and whatever another reader takes never reaches the engine. Replay Code that polls pygame directly cannot be replayed exactly. For sessions that replay ( --replay-trace ), read polled input from current_input() and take events through the engine; see Gameplay Recording and Replay . Code inside the glitchygames package must always do so ( tests/test_engine_doors.py ). What GlitchyGames adds on top of raw pygame: Named handlers — override on_key_down_event() instead of writing if event.type == pygame.KEYDOWN . No if/elif dispatch chains. Automatic state tracking — event managers cache button states, axis values, hat positions, and mouse focus so you can poll current state anytime. Synthesized events — GlitchyGames generates events that pygame doesn't provide: mouse drag and drop ( on_mouse_drag_event , on_left_mouse_drag_event , on_mouse_drop_event ), keyboard chords ( on_key_chord_down_event ), and per-button mouse events ( on_left_mouse_button_down_event vs raw MOUSEBUTTONDOWN with a button field). Custom event types — three engine-level event types ( FPSEVENT , GAMEEVENT , MENUEVENT ) built on pygame.USEREVENT offsets, plus an extensible GAMEEVENT bus for posting arbitrary game-specific events with per-subtype callbacks. An unhandled event safety net — every on_*_event() has a default stub that reports the event as unhandled (a warning once per type, or an UnhandledEventError under --no-unhandled-events ), and the engine counts every unhandled event type and logs the table at teardown. Events flow from SDL through pygame, into specialized event managers that track state and synthesize higher-level events, through the scene manager, and finally into scenes and sprites. Event Dispatch Overview # The complete path an event takes from SDL to your scene handler. The EVENT_HANDLERS dict provides O(1) lookup from pygame event type to the correct processing method. flowchart TD SDL["SDL2 Event Queue"] --> PG["active_sources().pump_events() (live: pygame.event.get())"] PG --> PE["GameEngine.process_events()"] PE -->|"scene defines process_event()"| RAW["scene.process_event(raw event)"] PE --> WRAP["HashableEvent.from_pygame()"] WRAP --> LOOKUP{"EVENT_HANDLERS [event.type]"} LOOKUP -->|"AUDIODEVICEADDED AUDIODEVICEREMOVED"| AUDIO["process_audio_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"CONTROLLERAXISMOTION CONTROLLERBUTTON* CONTROLLERDEVICE* CONTROLLERTOUCHPAD*"| CTRL["process_controller_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"DROPBEGIN DROPFILE DROPTEXT DROPCOMPLETE"| DROP["process_drop_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"KEYDOWN KEYUP"| KEY["process_keyboard_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"JOYAXISMOTION JOYBUTTON* JOYHAT* JOYBALL* JOYDEVICE*"| JOY["process_joystick_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"MOUSEMOTION MOUSEBUTTON* MOUSEWHEEL"| MOUSE["process_mouse_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"FINGERDOWN FINGERMOTION FINGERUP MULTIGESTURE"| TOUCH["process_touch_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"WINDOWEVENT WINDOW*"| WIN["process_window_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"FPSEVENT GAMEEVENT MENUEVENT QUIT USEREVENT ACTIVEEVENT VIDEO* SYSWMEVENT"| GAME["process_game_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"MIDIIN MIDIOUT"| MIDI["process_midi_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"TEXTEDITING TEXTINPUT"| TEXT["process_text_event()"] LOOKUP -->|"no entry, or not handled"| UNIMPL["process_unimplemented_event() counted in unhandled_events"] LOOKUP -->|"APP_*"| APP["process_app_event()"] AUDIO --> AM["AudioEventManager"] CTRL --> CM["ControllerEventManager"] DROP --> DM["DropEventManager"] KEY --> KM["KeyboardEventManager"] JOY --> JM["JoystickEventManager"] MOUSE --> MM["MouseEventManager"] TOUCH --> TM["TouchEventManager"] WIN --> WM["WindowEventManager"] GAME --> GM["GameEventManager"] MIDI --> MIM["MidiEventManager"] TEXT --> UNIMPL APP --> APM["AppEventManager"] AM & CM & DM & KM & JM & MM & TM & WM & GM & MIM & APM --> SM["SceneManager on_*_event()"] SM --> SCENE["Active Scene on_*_event()"] SCENE --> SPRITE["Focused/Collided Sprites on_*_event()"] Event performance tiers # Not all events pay the same cost. Events fall into three tiers depending on whether they're blocked, unhandled, or handled: flowchart TD EVT["SDL event fires"] --> BLOCKED{"Blocked by pygame.event.set_blocked?"} BLOCKED -->|"Yes"| ZERO["Filtered by SDL Never enters pipeline Cost: zero"] BLOCKED -->|"No"| WRAP["Wrap as HashableEvent O#40;1#41; EVENT_HANDLERS lookup"] WRAP --> STUB{"Scene overrides the handler?"} STUB -->|"No — hits stub"| UH["unhandled_event#40;#41; warns once per type#40;debug_events#41; or raises #40;no_unhandled_events#41;"] STUB -->|"Yes — real handler"| HANDLER["Your on_*_event#40;#41; runs Cost: dispatch + your code"] Tier When Cost per occurrence Example Blocked pygame.event.set_blocked(type) Zero — SDL filters it before the engine's pump Disabling MOUSEMOTION in a menu-only scene Unhandled The scene keeps the default stub Dispatch path + unhandled_event() : an options lookup, and a warning only for the type's first occurrence JOYAXISMOTION when no joystick handler exists Handled Scene overrides on_*_event() Full dispatch path + your handler executes on_key_down_event() processing a key press The EVENT_HANDLERS dict lookup is O(1) for all events that reach the pipeline, but every unblocked event still travels the dispatch path (wrap in HashableEvent , dict lookup, proxy forwarding). To eliminate that cost entirely, block the event at the pygame level with pygame.event.set_blocked() . Custom Event Types # GlitchyGames defines three custom event types beyond the standard pygame events, as fixed USEREVENT offsets ( USEREVENT + 1 , + 2 , + 3 ) rather than through pygame.event.custom_type() , so the engine's events have known, predictable numbers. Don't use pygame.event.custom_type() in a GlitchyGames game custom_type() hands out USEREVENT + 1 , + 2 , + 3 , ... in order, and nothing reserves the engine's offsets: in pygame-ce 2.5.8 the first three calls return the numbers of FPSEVENT , GAMEEVENT and MENUEVENT , so such an event would be dispatched as one of them. Use GAMEEVENT subtypes (below) instead. These constants are defined in glitchygames/events/base.py (exported by glitchygames.events ): FPSEVENT = pygame . USEREVENT + 1 # FPS counter updates GAMEEVENT = pygame . USEREVENT + 2 # Game-specific events (extensible via subtypes) MENUEVENT = pygame . USEREVENT + 3 # Menu item selections GAMEEVENT is intentionally generic — game code posts events with arbitrary payloads via GameEngine.post_game_event() , and can register per-subtype callbacks via GameEngine.register_game_event() (a scene reaches both through self.scene_manager : register_game_event() and game_engine ). This gives games an extensible event bus without consuming additional pygame event IDs. flowchart LR subgraph CustomEvents["Custom Event Types (fixed USEREVENT offsets)"] FPS["FPSEVENT pygame.USEREVENT + 1 FPS counter updates"] GAME_E["GAMEEVENT pygame.USEREVENT + 2 Game-specific events"] MENU["MENUEVENT pygame.USEREVENT + 3 Menu item selections"] end subgraph Producers["Producers"] SM_FPS["SceneManager posts every fps_log_interval_ms"] GAME_CODE["Game code posts via post_game_event()"] MENU_ITEM["MenuItem sprites post on click"] end subgraph Consumers["Consumers"] FPS_H["on_fps_event()"] GAME_H["on_game_event() + registered subtype callbacks"] MENU_H["on_menu_item_event()"] end SM_FPS --> FPS --> FPS_H GAME_CODE --> GAME_E --> GAME_H MENU_ITEM --> MENU --> MENU_H Extending GAMEEVENT in your game # GAMEEVENT is designed as an extensible event bus. Instead of consuming additional pygame event IDs for each game-specific event, you define integer subtypes and register callbacks for them. All subtypes share the single GAMEEVENT ID. Here's how a game might define custom events for a scoring system and a power-up system: # Define your game's event subtypes as constants SCORE_CHANGED = 1 POWER_UP_COLLECTED = 2 LEVEL_COMPLETE = 3 class MyGame ( Scene ): def setup ( self ): # Register callbacks for each subtype self . scene_manager . register_game_event ( SCORE_CHANGED , self . on_score_changed ) self . scene_manager . register_game_event ( POWER_UP_COLLECTED , self . on_power_up ) self . scene_manager . register_game_event ( LEVEL_COMPLETE , self . on_level_complete ) def on_score_changed ( self , event : HashableEvent ): new_score = event . score self . hud . update_score ( new_score ) def on_power_up ( self , event : HashableEvent ): power_type = event . power_type duration = event . duration self . player . apply_power_up ( power_type , duration ) def on_level_complete ( self , event : HashableEvent ): # The SceneManager switches to it after this frame self . next_scene = LevelTransitionScene ( event . next_level ) Any code in the game can fire these events: # From a collision handler, enemy class, pickup sprite, etc. # (SceneManager is a singleton: SceneManager().game_engine works anywhere) self . scene_manager . game_engine . post_game_event ( event_subtype = SCORE_CHANGED , event_data = { 'score' : self . score }, ) self . scene_manager . game_engine . post_game_event ( event_subtype = POWER_UP_COLLECTED , event_data = { 'power_type' : 'speed_boost' , 'duration' : 5.0 }, ) Under the hood, post_game_event creates a pygame.event.Event with type GAMEEVENT and a subtype field, then posts it with glitchygames.recording.post_event (so recordings mark it internal). SceneManager.on_game_event() looks up game_engine.registered_events[event.subtype] and calls the matching callback. If no callback is registered for that subtype, it logs an error telling you to call register_game_event() . This pattern gives you an unlimited number of game-specific event types while consuming only one pygame event ID. Native window messages (SYSWMEVENT) # SYSWMEVENT carries the window system's raw messages: on x11 every X event the window gets (focus, exposure, property and configure notifications), on Windows each window message ( hwnd , msg , wparam , lparam ). SDL leaves the type disabled, and so does the engine: GameEngine allows every event type through allow_every_event_type() ( glitchygames/events/base.py ), which keeps SYSWMEVENT blocked. Before, a plain pygame.event.set_allowed(None) turned it on, so on a real X server the queue, every --record-trace recording and every instant-replay journal filled with messages no game read. A game that wants them opts in on its scene class (the one given to GameEngine ), like TARGET_FPS : class MyGame ( Scene ): NATIVE_WINDOW_MESSAGES = True # anything but a bool is refused with TypeError def on_sys_wm_event ( self , event : HashableEvent ) -> None : # A plain HashableEvent (SYSWMEVENT has no class in EVENT_CLASSES) holding # pygame's platform fields: event.event (the raw XEvent bytes) on x11 ... The route is GameEngine.process_game_event → GameEventManager.on_sys_wm_event → SceneManager → the active scene's on_sys_wm_event . A game that opts in records them like any other event (an x11 message's bytes are stored as {"__bytes__": ""} ), and a replay serves the recorded ones; a replay's input blocking ( glitchygames/replay/input_blocking.py ) restores the type to blocked when it ends. pygame-ce 2.5.8 reports SYSWMEVENT as allowed until something blocks it through pygame, although SDL ignores it, which is why the engine blocks it explicitly: a snapshot-and-restore of the blocked types would otherwise turn it on. The proxy chain provides two capabilities: Event dispatch : When GameEngine calls on_*_event() on an event manager (e.g., MouseEventManager ), the event manager forwards to its inner proxy, which updates internal state (tracking pressed keys, button states, drag sequences, etc.) and then forwards the event to self.game — the active scene. Attribute fallthrough : An attribute the manager doesn't have is looked up on its proxies by ResourceManager.__getattr__ ( glitchygames/events/base.py ). The design is that mouse_manager.get_pos() falls through the inner proxy and the scene to pygame.mouse . Only the first proxy is consulted ResourceManager.__getattr__ returns (or raises) on the first proxy in self.proxies , so the lookup stops at self.game : MouseEventManager().get_pos() raises AttributeError unless the scene has get_pos . The pygame modules in the proxy lists below are never reached. Polled input should come from glitchygames.input.state.current_input() anyway: it is the frame's snapshot, which a replay serves exactly. Why this matters : Scenes and sprites never need a direct reference to the event plumbing. They talk to the event manager, which is a singleton accessible from anywhere, and the manager handles state tracking (what buttons are held, what sprite has mouse focus, what keys form a chord). Architecture # Each manager follows the same two-layer structure: MouseEventManager (singleton ResourceManager) ├── proxies: [MouseEventProxy] │ └── MouseEventProxy (inner class, also a ResourceManager) ├── proxies: [self.game, pygame.mouse] ├── state: mouse_state, dragging, focus tracking └── on_*_event(): update state, synthesize events, forward to self.game The inner proxy holds the real state and logic. The outer manager is just a singleton wrapper that ensures only one proxy chain exists per subsystem.
